transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-09
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Evan Cho (Redwood Solutions Eng); Mark Li (Sapphire CTO), Lila Hernandez (Platform), Robert Greene (Security), Aisha Khan (SRE)
---
Summary:
Quick demo of Redwood Console quota/guardrail patterns focused on multi-tenant routing, per-project and org keys, sticky routing for latency-sensitive tenants, and fallback behavior for burst periods. Discussed compliance (SOC2), KMS, and pilot next steps.
Topics:
- Project-key zoning and quotas
- Sticky routing and fairshare during spikes
- Burst cushions and reserved capacity patterns
- Data residency and KMS integration
- Pilot scope and benchmarks
Action items and next steps summarized at end.
---
Transcript (timestamps approximate):
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this to about 45 to 60 minutes. I'm Jordan from Redwood, with Priya and Evan. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Mark: Doing good. Thanks. We have about an hour, so that works.
[00:12] Jordan: Great. Quick agenda: Priya will demo the Console route and quota setup then we'll show an example policy for sticky routing and a pilot plan. We'll leave time for security and SRE questions. Sound ok?
[00:23] Lila: Yes, perfect.
[00:26] Priya: Alright jumping in — I'm going to share my screen, you'll see the Console. If anyone can't see say so.
[00:35] Aisha: We can see it. Audio's good.
[00:38] [00:40] Priya: First thing, we have a tenant segmentation view. You can see org-level keys and within them project keys. So for Sapphire we might have an org key for the whole company and project keys for internal apps: search-api, customer-chat, and metrics-ingest.
[00:56] Mark: That's the model we use today, one token per service, sometimes per environment.
[01:00] Priya: Cool, this maps well. In the Console you can create quota buckets per project key — I can pick rate per second, monthly token caps, and concurrency ceilings. For latency-sensitive services like customer-chat we normally set a lower concurrency with sticky routing to warm caches — that keeps KV cache hot on specific replicas.
[01:25] Robert: When you say sticky routing — does that mean we pin requests from a project to a specific pool? How does that affect failover?
[01:33] Priya: Good question. Sticky routing pins by project key to a pool or subset of instances to preserve warmed KV cache and reduce cold-token latency. It's paired with a fallback policy: if reserved pool is saturated, requests can be routed to a compatible model in a different pool or degraded variant — you can set automatic fallback or manual.
[01:52] Evan: And the Console shows expected latency impact and cost delta when you toggle these policies, so you can see tradeoffs live.
[01:58] Mark: Nice. We care about 95th pct latency for chat being under 180ms. Are you showing absolute numbers?
[02:05] Evan: The Console pull is based on your workload profile; for demonstration we use Redwood-verified model benchmarks. In a pilot we'll run your traces for more accurate numbers.
[02:12] [02:15] Priya: Let me click into quota rules — here's a rule per project key, you can attach a policy: rate limit of X rps, burst cushion of Y tokens, and a monthly cap. We also have concurrency quotas by route.
[02:29] Lila: About burst cushions — if we get a sudden spike from a scheduled job, can those tokens be borrowed across projects? We have a shared billing org but want isolation most of the time.
[02:37] Priya: Yes. Two options: elastic pool where projects draw from a shared cushion with per-project soft limits; or isolated slices where projects can't borrow. You can mix both with priority weights — fairshare allocation. So scheduled jobs could have low priority to avoid displacing chat.
[02:54] Mark: Do you support dynamic adjustments? For example, IDS triggering causes a traffic surge and we'd like auto-bursting for short windows.
[02:59] Priya: We support time-bound burst windows — you can configure burst allowances with TTL and a max refill rate. Also policy hooks support telemetry triggers — so an autoscaler or firewall event can hit our API to increase a cushion temporarily.
[03:12] Robert: Regarding security, how are audit logs and identity handled? We must show SOC2 logs for each API key usage, and SSO is mandatory.
[03:19] Jordan: We support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, role-based access control, and per-key audit trails. Logs include request metadata, model variants, and routing decisions. You can export to your SIEM via syslog or push to S3 with encryption.
[03:32] Robert: KMS? Our keys must be handled by our HSM in cloud provider.
[03:36] Jordan: We integrate with AWS KMS and HSM-backed CMKs; for private deployments you can bring-your-own-HSM. We'll share the architecture diagram in the follow-up link.
[03:44] [03:50] Priya: Back to the demo — here's a policy editor. I'll create a policy named "chat-priority" that pins the project key to the low-latency pool, sets an rps of 80, concurrency 30, burst cushion 250 tokens, and fallback to a quantized model variant if thresholds exceed.
[04:07] Priya: Notice the policy feedback panel — it estimates cost delta (about +12%) and expected 95p latency improvement.
[04:15] Aisha: That estimate — is it based on total tokens or per-request? We need to map to our billing model which is per-1000 tokens.
[04:21] Evan: It's token-aware. The Console models both per-token cost and instance-level costs so you see the per-request and per-hour delta.
[04:28] Mark: We also need pinned capacity for peak hours — reserved capacity or dedicated pools?
[04:33] Priya: Reserved capacity (Dedicated) is the right pattern if you want guaranteed throughput. You can define a reserved pool and route keys to it. There's also a hybrid guardrail: a reserved baseline plus burst to shared cloud capacity as overflow.
[04:47] Mark: If we do reserved baseline plus overflow, how do you charge?
[04:51] Jordan: Pricing mixes a flat reserved cost and usage for overflow. We'll share sample pricing scenarios in the follow-up.
[04:57] [05:00] Robert: On encryption in transit — do you support mTLS between our VPC and your private runtime?
[05:05] Jordan: For Redwood Private we support mTLS, VPC peering, and private link. For hosted we use TLS with mutual auth options for enterprise.
[05:13] Priya: Next I'll show routing rules. You can build a route that says: if project-key==customer-chat AND time-window within 9-17 (region SST) then route to pool-low-latency; else route to pool-cost-optimized.
[05:26] Lila: Can those rules be weighted? We want 80/20 split during migration periods.
[05:30] Priya: Yep, weighted routing is supported, including percent-based rollout and canary by project or by header token.
[05:36] [05:40] Evan: One neat feature is cost-aware routing. Suppose you have a cheaper quantized variant that meets quality thresholds for most users — you can route lower-risk traffic there and only route high-value sessions to the high-cost model.
[05:53] Mark: How do you determine "risk"?
[05:55] Evan: You can use request tags, user cohorts, or prompt length thresholds. We also support hooking an external decision service via a function-call so your business logic can steer routing.
[06:06] Robert: We need to capture routing decisions for audits. Is that logged per request?
[06:09] Priya: Yes, routing decision is in the request metadata and audit logs. The trace shows which pool, model variant, and fallback if any.
[06:16] [06:20] Priya: Switching to API demo — the same policies are exposed via REST. You can create policy objects: quota, route, fallback. Here's a sample curl to create a quota rule for project-key "search-api".
[06:32] Priya: curl -X POST /v1/policies -d '{"type":"quota","project":"search-api","rps":50,"burst":100}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer ...'
[06:40] Mark: Ok we like API-first controls for IaC. Do you provide Terraform or Helm modules?
[06:44] Jordan: We have a Terraform provider in beta, and a Helm chart for Private. We can include example modules in the pilot repo.
[06:52] [07:00] Aisha: For the pilot, we want to run a 2-week test with our synthetic traffic at 2k qps and a small proportion of real traffic. Can Redwood run that in our VPC?
[07:09] Priya: Yes for Private deployment or a dedicated VPC peering for the pilot. We usually recommend starting with dedicated pools and a traffic mirror for safety.
[07:17] Mark: About SLA — we need 99.9 for inference endpoints. Is that in Dedicated?
[07:23] Jordan: SLA tiers are available on Dedicated contracts; hosted API has a best-effort tier with credits, but Dedicated includes stricter uptime guarantees. We'll include SLA options in the proposal.
[07:31] [07:35] Priya: Now quick look at Optimize suggestions — the Optimize tab has recommended quantization profiles by workload. For your metrics-ingest, it suggests int8 with 4k context, estimated 2x cost reduction. For chat, conservative int8 + KV cache is suggested to hit your 95p target.
[07:52] Mark: Can Optimize trigger automatic rollouts? We don't want surprises.
[07:56] Priya: Optimize creates suggestions only; rollouts are manual unless you opt-in for auto-apply with a safety threshold and canaries.
[08:03] Evan: We also support tests: you can run an A/B on a set of prompts and measure quality drift. If drift exceeds threshold, roll back automatically.
[08:12] [08:20] Robert: A few compliance specifics — we need retention controls on logs (90 days), ability to purge request bodies on demand, and encryption keys that we control.
[08:30] Jordan: Those are supported: log retention configurable per customer, selective data purge via API (subject to retention policy), and BYOK/KMS integration for Private.
[08:38] Lila: For data residency, we need EU-only processing for EU customers.
[08:43] Priya: You can pin models and pools to regions; routing can be region-aware. For the pilot we can route EU traffic to EU-only pools.
[08:52] [09:00] Mark: Sounds good. What about cost predictions? We need monthly forecasts if we enable sticky routing for chat.
[09:05] Evan: We'll run your sample trace and produce a per-project cost forecast with scenarios for sticky routing, reserved capacity, and quantization.
[09:12] [09:20] Jordan: I'll summarize recommended pilot: 2-week pilot, dedicated pool for chat with sticky routing, shared elastic cushion for batch jobs, run 2k qps synthetic trace plus 5% real traffic, measure 95p latency and cost delta.
[09:33] Mark: Agree.
[09:35] Aisha: Timeline?
[09:37] Jordan: Propose kickoff week of 2026-05-19, run for two weeks, and 1-hour benchmarking session before ramp.
[09:44] [09:50] Priya: Any final technical questions?
[09:52] Robert: One—if fallback hits quantized variant, how do you surface quality regressions to us?
[09:56] Priya: We tag responses with model_variant and quality score metrics; Optimize can run prompt-level evaluation and trigger regression alerts tied to prompt sets.
[10:06] Mark: Can we get examples of the policies in JSON/YAML?
[10:09] Jordan: Yes, we'll include sample YAML for project-key zoning and a recommended quota matrix.
[10:14] Lila: Also include a network diagram for Private deployment and the KMS flow.
[10:18] Jordan: Noted.
[10:20] [10:25] Evan: I'll capture the pilot runbook items and a checklist: preflight checks, synthetic trace, perf dashboards, rollback steps.
[10:33] Mark: That's helpful.
[10:35] Jordan: Ok last callouts — pricing scenarios, SOC2 docs, and sample Terraform provider will be in the follow-up. We'll send a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff once dates are locked.
[10:46] Mark: Thanks everyone.
[10:48] Robert: Thank you.
[10:50] Jordan: Thanks, bye.
